title: GOP Congressman Calls His Own Atlanta District an H-1B Fraud 'Hotspot,' Seeks Federal Probe
excerpt: Rep. Rich McCormick's letter to the Trump administration lands amid the most aggressive H-1B enforcement campaign in the program's history, with a nationwide fraud probe and a 48% surge in investigations.
body:
• Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., is writing to the Trump administration on Tuesday asking for a federal investigation into alleged H-1B visa fraud in his own district, which he called a "suspected hotspot of this fraud."
  • McCormick, who represents Georgia's 7th District covering Atlanta's northern suburbs, offered himself as "an interlocutor to help enable cooperation with state-level agencies and law enforcement."
  • His letter argues the H-1B program has become the subject of "rampant fraud and abuse," with workers exploited through below-market wages and abusive conditions tied to their dependence on employers for legal status.
  • What it means for H-1B holders: the letter lands amid an unprecedented enforcement wave — a federal judge struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee as an unconstitutional tax, the Labor Department's Inspector General is running a nationwide fraud probe, and a "Project Firewall" initiative has driven a reported 48% surge in investigations.

A Republican congressman is asking the Trump administration to investigate alleged H-1B visa fraud in his own backyard. Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., is writing to the administration on Tuesday requesting a federal probe into abuse of the foreign-worker visa program in Georgia's 7th Congressional District — and warning that the Atlanta suburbs he represents are a "suspected hotspot of this fraud."

The letter

McCormick's district encompasses part of the Atlanta metro area, including the city's northern suburbs and part of Fulton County. In the letter, he offered himself as "an interlocutor to help enable cooperation with state-level agencies and law enforcement," signalling he wants federal investigators working directly with Georgia authorities.

https://x.com/foxnewspolitics/status/2107610618677391495

The congressman framed the program's original purpose before turning to its alleged abuses. "Established by the Immigration Act of 1990, the purpose of the H-1B program is to allow American businesses to temporarily bring in foreign citizens to fill key, high-skill employment positions when the domestic workforce demonstrably cannot provide the necessary labor," he wrote. "Unfortunately, the H-1B program has become the subject of rampant fraud and abuse for the nefarious purposes of obtaining labor that bad actors can exploit" through "below-market-rate wages and abusive work conditions given H-1B holders' dependence on retaining their employment in order to avoid removal back to their country of origin."

He argued the alleged fraud is "sowing uncertainty in the U.S. labor market by undercutting wages and unfairly increasing competition for American workers, particularly those fresh out of college."

An enforcement wave

McCormick's letter arrives in the middle of the most aggressive H-1B enforcement campaign in the program's history. The Labor Department's Office of Inspector General is conducting a nationwide investigation into fraud, worker exploitation and possible human trafficking connected to foreign-labour programs — a probe that has already produced enforcement actions, with Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito warning of significant changes to come.

Under the "Project Firewall" initiative, federal investigators have shifted from complaint-driven probes to proactive, data-driven cases, with one report citing a 48% surge in investigations. The September 18 executive order directed the Departments of Labor, Homeland Security and State to consider whether an employer has laid off similarly situated U.S. workers when reviewing H-1B applications, and the State Department under Marco Rubio launched a "Report Visa Fraud" portal inviting the public to submit tips.

Meanwhile, the administration's $100,000 H-1B fee — the centrepiece of its overhaul — was struck down by a federal judge who ruled it an unconstitutional tax, though the administration has moved to extend restrictions and codify similar measures by rule through September 2027.

"The H-1B program has become the subject of rampant fraud and abuse for the nefarious purposes of obtaining labor that bad actors can exploit."

— Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga.

Diaspora angle

For the tens of thousands of Indian professionals on H-1B visas — Indians are by far the program's largest beneficiaries — the Atlanta development is a double-edged signal. Fraud probes that target exploitative body-shop operators could, in principle, help legitimate workers. But the political framing of the program as "rampant" with fraud, coming from a congressman whose own district hosts major Indian-American tech communities, adds to an atmosphere in which every H-1B holder faces heightened scrutiny: more frequent site visits, broader workforce audits, and employers growing reluctant to sponsor. Workers in the Atlanta metro area should expect compliance reviews to intensify and keep documentation — pay stubs, job descriptions, work location records — current.

What's next

It remains to be seen whether the administration acts on McCormick's request for a district-level investigation, but the political logic is clear: a Republican lawmaker inviting scrutiny of his own district gives the White House cover to deepen enforcement without accusations of partisanship. With the DOL Inspector General's probe ongoing and courts still weighing the fee fight, the H-1B landscape heading into 2027 looks set to be defined less by legislation and more by investigation.
